about: Historical-tendency rules researched 2026-11-24. Threshold provenance: SOURCE = stated by the cited source; CONVENTION = market practice; APP_HEURISTIC = app default, never presented as sourced. Citations marked verified=known were not re-checked in research and are not displayed.

R01.measures: Slope of the Treasury curve. Reflects expected policy path (2Y) vs long-run growth/inflation + term premium (10Y).
R01.normal_range: Positive most of the time. Inverted (<0) in the late cycle before most post-1970 US recessions.
R01.threshold_provenance: CONVENTION (zero line); the Fed literature prefers 3m10y
R01.implies: Historically associated with markets pricing future policy easing and a higher probability of recession over the following 6-24 months. Pressure on bank NIM expectations.
R01.sentence: The 2s10s curve is inverted at {level}bp. Historically, inversions have preceded most US recessions, but with long and variable lags (often 6-24 months), and the 2022-24 inversion was not followed by a recession within that window.
caveats: Lead time is long and variable
2s10s inverts more often and less decisively than 3m10y (FRBSF 2022)
QE-compressed term premium can flatten the curve without signalling recession (Engstrom & Sharpe 2018)

R02.measures: The NY Fed's preferred curve slope for its 12-month-ahead recession probability (probit, Estrella-Mishkin).
R02.threshold_provenance: SOURCE for the zero line and the NY Fed probit. 30% is a CONVENTION often cited as 'elevated'; treat it as APP_HEURISTIC
R02.implies: Historically the most reliable single market-based recession predictor in Fed research.
R02.sentence: The 3m10y spread is {level}bp. In NY Fed and FRBSF research, a negative 3m10y slope has historically preceded US recessions with a lag of roughly 6-24 months. The model output is a probability, not a forecast.
caveats: The 2022-24 inversion was the longest on record without a recession inside the typical window
Term premium distortion: a 'real' spread version gave lower probabilities in 2023 (St. Louis Fed)

R03.indicator: 2s10s or 3m10y crossing back above zero after an inversion
R03.condition: min_spread_prior_24m_bp < 0 AND spread_bp crosses > 0 AND driven by 2Y falling (bull steepening)
R03.implies: Historically the curve has often re-steepened, mostly via falling front-end yields as the Fed cuts, around or shortly before recession onsets. The 'all clear' reading is therefore historically unreliable.
R03.sentence: The curve has dis-inverted to {level}bp, led by a {chg_2y}bp fall in 2Y yields. Historically, bull re-steepening after an inversion has often coincided with Fed easing near the start of downturns rather than signalling the all-clear.
caveats: Small sample (about 8 US cycles)
Re-steepening driven by term premium (bear steepening) has a different meaning; see R04

implies.BULL_STEEPENER: Markets pricing nearer/faster Fed cuts. Often growth-scare or easing.
implies.BEAR_STEEPENER: Long-end selloff from term premium, supply or inflation worries. Can tighten financial conditions (2023 'Treasury tantrum').
implies.BULL_FLATTENER: Long-end rally on growth/inflation worries or flight to quality.
implies.BEAR_FLATTENER: Front end repricing for a more hawkish Fed. Typical of hiking cycles.

R04.sentence: The curve moved in a {type} pattern: 2Y {chg_2y}bp and 10Y {chg_10y}bp. Historically, {type_meaning}.
caveats: Single-day classification is noisy; prefer 5-day
Supply/auction days can produce mechanical bear steepening

R05.threshold_provenance: APP_HEURISTIC (10bp is a desk convention; use z-score as primary)
R05.implies: Large up-moves tighten financial conditions: pressure on long-duration equities (growth/tech), small caps, REITs, mortgage rates. Large down-moves on weak data are a growth scare. Bond markets react most strongly to macro news among asset classes.
R05.sentence: The 10Y yield moved {chg}bp ({z} standard deviations). Historically, moves of this size tied to macro news have shown up first and most strongly in bonds, with the equity reaction depending on whether the driver is growth news or inflation/policy news.
caveats: Sign of equity reaction depends on the driver (growth vs discount-rate shock) and the business-cycle state (Andersen et al.)

R06.measures: Inflation-adjusted return on 10Y Treasuries; the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets (gold) and a key discount-rate input for equities.
R06.normal_range: Roughly -1% to +2.5% since 2003 (check the live series)
R06.implies: Historically gold has been negatively correlated with real yields (Erb & Harvey report a strong negative correlation between 10Y TIPS yields and the real gold price). Higher real yields also weigh on long-duration equities.
R06.sentence: 10Y real yields rose {chg}bp over {window}. Historically, rising real yields have been associated with weaker gold and long-duration equities, but since 2022 heavy central-bank gold buying has weakened the gold link.
caveats: Correlation is not causation (Erb & Harvey)
2022-2026: gold rallied despite high real yields, linked to EM central-bank purchases and sanctions risk (IMF)

R07.measures: Market-implied inflation compensation = expected inflation + inflation risk premium - TIPS liquidity premium.
R07.normal_range: Roughly 2.0-2.5% in 'anchored' periods; well below 2% in deflation scares (2008, 2020)
R07.condition: chg_be10y_bp_20d >= +20 OR be5y5y moves outside its 2y range (APP_HEURISTIC)
R07.implies: Rising breakevens: reflation (commodities, cyclicals, TIPS outperform nominals) or a de-anchoring worry (hawkish Fed risk). Falling breakevens with falling oil: disinflation or growth scare.
R07.sentence: 10Y breakevens moved {chg}bp to {level}%. Historically, breakevens track oil and growth expectations closely. Because they also embed liquidity and risk premia, the Fed pays most attention to longer-horizon measures such as 5y5y.
caveats: TIPS liquidity distortions, especially in crises (Cleveland Fed)
Highly correlated with oil at short horizons

R08.measures: Extra compensation for holding long bonds vs rolling short bills. Model-dependent.
R08.condition: chg_10y_bp_20d >= 25 AND share of move from TP >= 50%
R08.implies: A term-premium-driven rise in yields (supply, fiscal, uncertainty) tightens financial conditions without implying a more hawkish Fed path. In 2023 it followed Treasury's issuance surprise.
R08.sentence: Most of the {chg}bp rise in 10Y yields is attributed to term premium in the {model} model. Historically, term-premium-driven selloffs (e.g. Aug-Oct 2023) have reflected supply and uncertainty rather than Fed expectations. Model estimates differ widely.
caveats: Models can disagree on sign and size: at the Oct 2023 peak ACM about 0.46, KW about 0.39, CR about 1.37 (Fed note)
Revised and estimated, not observed

R09.measures: Market-implied probabilities of FOMC outcomes (fed funds futures price = 100 - expected avg EFFR).
R09.condition: |chg_implied_cuts_bp_1d| >= 15 (APP_HEURISTIC, i.e. more than half a cut repriced) OR prob_next_meeting crosses 50%
R09.implies: Dovish repricing: front-end rally, bull steepening, weaker USD, small caps and gold supported. Hawkish: the reverse.
R09.sentence: Futures now price {cuts}bp of cuts over 12 months, a {chg}bp change on the day. These are market-implied probabilities under CME's method, not forecasts, and they have historically swung sharply on payrolls and CPI surprises.
caveats: Embeds risk premia, so not a pure expectation
FedWatch's conditional vs aggregated views differ (CME 2024)

R10.measures: Implied normal yield volatility from 1-month options on 2/5/10/30Y Treasuries. Direction-neutral.
R10.normal_range: Ranged from about 55 (late 2025) to about 115 (early 2026) per Schwab. 2008 peak about 265.
R10.implies: High rates vol tends to coincide with wider credit/MBS spreads, worse Treasury liquidity, and reduced risk-taking (dealer balance-sheet VaR).
R10.sentence: The MOVE index is {level} ({pctile} percentile). Elevated Treasury volatility has historically coincided with tighter financial conditions and wider mortgage and credit spreads. It measures expected swing size, not direction.
caveats: Methodology proprietary (ICE)
Can stay elevated for long periods in hiking cycles

R11.indicator: Auction stop vs when-issued (tail), bid-to-cover, indirect share
R11.condition: tail_bp >= 1.0 AND btc < btc_avg_6 (APP_HEURISTIC). Stop-through: tail_bp <= -1.0
R11.threshold_provenance: APP_HEURISTIC (desk convention compares against the 6-auction average)
R11.implies: Weak long-end auctions have been associated with intraday long-end selloffs and bear steepening, especially in heavy-supply / term-premium regimes. Older evidence: yields tend to rise into auctions and fall after (supply concession).
R11.sentence: The {tenor} auction tailed {tail}bp with bid-to-cover of {btc}x vs a {btc_avg}x average. Historically, weak auctions have produced short-lived long-end selloffs, and the market impact usually fades within days unless it confirms a broader supply-driven trend.
caveats: Effects are mostly transitory
Indirect bidder category is a noisy proxy for foreign demand

R12.indicator: Reserve balances (WRESBAL), ON RRP usage (RRPONTSYD), Fed balance sheet (WALCL), TGA
R12.measures: System liquidity. Falling reserves/RRP buffers during QT can create money-market strain.
R12.condition: sofr_minus_iorb_bp > 0 for several days OR reserves fall sharply around tax dates/quarter-end with rrp near zero
R12.threshold_provenance: APP_HEURISTIC. The NY Fed says there is no fixed number for 'ample' reserves
R12.implies: In Sept 2019 reserves fell to about $1.34tn around the corporate tax date + heavy Treasury settlement, and repo rates spiked, prompting Fed repo operations and bill purchases.
R12.sentence: Reserves are {level}bn and ON RRP is {rrp}bn. Historically, when RRP buffers are depleted and repo rates trade above the IORB rate, money-market strain has followed (Sept 2019), often prompting Fed action.
caveats: No fixed 'ample' threshold (NY Fed)
Standing Repo Facility (2021) changes the dynamics

R13.implies: BIS: the broad dollar acts as a barometer of global risk-taking capacity. A stronger dollar has been associated with tighter global financial conditions, less cross-border USD lending, weaker EM growth outlooks (1pp dollar appreciation -> EM growth outlook down >0.3pp), and historically lower commodity prices.
R13.sentence: The dollar is up {chg}% over {window}. In BIS research, broad dollar strength has historically coincided with tighter global financial conditions and weaker emerging-market assets.
caveats: The oil-dollar correlation turned positive after 2020 as the US became a net energy exporter (IMF 2024)
The dollar can rise on US growth outperformance (benign) or on a flight to safety (risk-off)

R14.implies: Funding-currency spikes (yen) with high-yielders falling (MXN, EM FX) have marked carry-trade unwinds. Volatility amplified by procyclical deleveraging and margin calls (Aug 2024: TOPIX -12% on 5 Aug; BIS estimated about ¥40tn / $250bn of FX carry positions).
R14.sentence: The yen has strengthened {chg}% in {window} while volatility is rising. Historically, abrupt yen rallies have coincided with carry-trade unwinds that hit high-yielding EM currencies and crowded equity trades. The August 2024 episode was sharp but short-lived.
caveats: Carry positioning is hard to measure (BIS)
BoJ communication can quickly stabilise markets

citations.verified: known (Brunnermeier, Nagel, Pedersen: Carry Trades and Currency Crashes)

R15.condition: oil_ret_20d_pct >= +20 OR oil makes a new 3-year high (Hamilton's 'net oil price increase' concept)
R15.threshold_provenance: SOURCE for the concept (Hamilton's net oil price increase over the prior 3-year max). The 20% figure is APP_HEURISTIC
R15.implies: Hamilton: oil price increases matter much more than decreases (nonlinear). Large increases above recent highs have preceded most postwar US recessions, by disrupting consumer and firm spending. Short-run: higher breakevens, energy outperforms, airlines/consumer discretionary underperform, bear-flattening risk if the Fed is hawkish.
R15.sentence: Oil is up {chg}% over {window} to {level}. Historically, large oil price increases, especially to new multi-year highs, have weighed on consumer spending and preceded several US recessions. Declines have had a smaller, less reliable effect.
caveats: The US is now a net petroleum exporter, so the domestic impact is more mixed
Demand-driven oil rallies (strong growth) differ from supply shocks

R16.implies: Backwardation is associated with tight physical markets and low inventories (supports prompt prices, inflation pressure). Contango with oversupply and high inventories (storage pays). Super-contango (Apr 2020) signals storage stress.
R16.sentence: The oil curve is in {state} ({spread} USD M1-M12). Historically, backwardation has reflected tight supply and low inventories, while contango has reflected oversupply. Curve shape describes current balances, not future prices.
caveats: Geopolitical risk can steepen backwardation without a lasting inventory change

R17.implies: Historically co-moved with the 10Y yield (cyclical growth vs safety). Popularised as a short-term yield indicator. A falling ratio has been read as a growth-scare signal.
R17.sentence: The copper/gold ratio moved {chg}% while 10Y yields moved {chg10}bp. The ratio historically tracked Treasury yields, but the relationship has largely broken down since 2021 as central-bank gold buying lifted gold, so treat divergences cautiously.
caveats: Correlation broke down after 2021 (CFA Institute, MNI)
Academic support limited to very short horizons

R18.implies: Drivers per IMF/ECB: safe-haven demand in uncertainty, opportunity cost (real rates, Fed funds), sanctions-related central-bank reserve diversification. ECB finds safe-haven behaviour in stress. IMF notes this is unreliable in tail events.
R18.sentence: Gold is up {chg}% ({context}). Historically, gold strength has reflected falling real rates, a weaker dollar, geopolitical or policy uncertainty, and, since 2022, heavy central-bank buying. Its safe-haven behaviour in sharp selloffs has been inconsistent.
caveats: Erb & Harvey (2025): returns after all-time highs have often been low over multi-year horizons
Gold can fall in liquidity scrambles (March 2020)

R19.implies: IMF: BTC-S&P 500 daily correlation rose from 0.01 (2017-19) to 0.36 (2020-21). BTC volatility explained about 1/6 of S&P volatility during the pandemic. BTC has behaved as a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge.
R19.sentence: Bitcoin moved {chg}% with a 60-day S&P correlation of {corr}. Since 2020, IMF research finds crypto has traded more like a high-beta risk asset than a hedge, so large crypto moves have often accompanied broader risk appetite shifts.
caveats: Correlation is window-dependent and unstable
Crypto-specific events (ETF flows, hacks, regulation) dominate at times
Trades 24/7, so weekend moves can lead Monday's equity open

R20.normal_range: Long-term median about 17.6 (Cboe). Since 1990 mostly 13-25 (20th-80th pct), mean about 19.5. Post-major-decline average about 37 (Cboe).
R20.threshold_provenance: CONVENTION. Bands bracket Cboe's 17.6 median and the 13/25 percentiles. 30+ approximates stress regimes (Cboe post-decline avg 37)
R20.implies: VIX is mean-reverting (Cboe). Low VIX is calm but can coincide with leverage build-up (BIS: positions built in calm periods unwind fast). VIX >= 30 historically clusters with drawdowns and wider credit spreads, and also with elevated subsequent returns on average.
R20.sentence: VIX is {level}, versus a long-run median near 17.6 (Cboe). Historically, readings {band_text} have been associated with {band_meaning}. VIX tends to mean-revert, but timing is unreliable.
caveats: Implied vol embeds a risk premium (usually above realized)
Spikes can be brief (Aug 2024) or persistent (2008)

R21.sentence: VIX jumped {chg} points ({chg_pct}%). Historically, sharp one-day volatility spikes reflect a rush for downside protection. Many fade within days, while those accompanied by credit widening have tended to last longer.
caveats: Percentage change exaggerates moves from low bases

R22.indicator: VIX / VIX3M ratio (or VIX futures M1 vs M2)
R22.threshold_provenance: SOURCE for the concept (Cboe: contango is normal; backwardation occurred <20% of the time since 2010). 1.0 is definitional. 0.9 is a community convention (APP_HEURISTIC)
R22.implies: Near-term fear exceeds medium-term. Historically coincides with acute selloffs.
R22.sentence: Front-month implied volatility ({vix}) exceeds 3-month ({vix3m}), an inverted term structure. Cboe data show this has happened less than 20% of the time since 2010 and marks acute stress, but Cboe notes it has not reliably predicted further declines outside the largest selloffs.
caveats: Often coincident with, or late to, the selloff; sometimes near capitulation lows
Cboe explicitly warns backwardation is not necessarily a sign of a future down market

R23.indicator: ICE BofA US High Yield OAS
R23.normal_range: Recent: about 2.7% (Aug 2026) to 3.2% (12 Nov 2026) per FRED. The Fed FSR (Nov 2025) described spreads as well below historical medians.

condition.HY_DISTRESS_SIGNAL: S&P distress ratio (share of HY issues > 1,000bp OAS) rising

R23.threshold_provenance: 1,000bp = SOURCE (Fridson/S&P distress definition). Percentile bands = APP_HEURISTIC computed from history. 600bp = APP_HEURISTIC
R23.implies: Tight spreads = strong risk appetite and open markets for issuers. Fed research (López-Salido, Stein, Zakrajšek): narrow spreads + high junk issuance share have historically preceded slower growth 2-3 years later. Wide spreads = tighter credit supply.
R23.sentence: HY spreads are {level}bp ({pctile} percentile of history). Historically, very tight spreads have reflected strong risk appetite. Fed research finds that unusually tight spreads with heavy junk issuance have preceded slower growth a few years later, while sharp widening has preceded weaker activity.
caveats: Index composition has shifted to higher quality (more BB) over time, so raw levels are not fully comparable
FRED now shows only 3 years of history (from Apr 2026); source full history from ICE

R24.implies: Gilchrist-Zakrajšek: unexpected increases in bond spreads, especially the excess bond premium, have been followed by large and persistent contractions in activity, signalling reduced risk-bearing capacity and less credit supply.
R24.sentence: HY spreads widened {chg}bp over {window}. In Fed research, rapid spread widening beyond what default risk explains (the excess bond premium) has historically preceded tighter credit supply and weaker economic activity.
caveats: Technical (fund-flow) widening can reverse quickly
EBP history revises monthly

R25.implies: IG widening raises funding costs for investment-grade issuers (M&A bridge takeouts, buybacks). It is less default-driven than HY and more sensitive to supply, rates vol and foreign demand.
R25.sentence: IG spreads moved {chg}bp to {level}bp. Historically, IG spreads widen with rate volatility and heavy supply as well as with growth fears. Sustained widening has raised borrowing costs for investment-grade acquirers.
caveats: Supply-heavy weeks (e.g. jumbo M&A deals) widen spreads mechanically

R26.indicator: HYG and LQD ETF prices; HYG/IEF ratio
R26.implies: Intraday proxy for credit risk appetite when cash-bond OAS is stale. HYG excess return vs Treasuries isolates spread moves.
R26.sentence: HYG underperformed Treasuries by {spread_ret}% today. Credit ETFs give a real-time read on risk appetite. In stress (e.g. March 2020) they have traded at discounts to NAV, which can overstate cash-bond moves.
caveats: ETF price includes rate duration, so hedge with IEF
NAV discounts are liquidity effects, not pure credit

citations.title: BIS Bulletin 6: Recent distress in corporate bond markets, cues from ETFs
NBER w27168: corporate bond market stress in March 2020

R27.implies: Fed research: credit spreads contain information about future activity beyond what equity prices hold (Gilchrist-Yankov-Zakrajšek). Stock-market sentiment has little predictive power for real activity (López-Salido et al.).
R27.sentence: Equities are near highs while HY spreads have widened {chg}bp. Fed research finds credit spreads carry information about future activity that stock prices do not. Evidence that credit leads stock prices at short horizons, however, is mixed.
caveats: Lead-lag between bond and stock returns is inconclusive in the academic literature (Tolikas 2018)

R28.implies: Narrow rallies (index up, few participants) are often read as fragile. Washouts often occur near selloff lows.
R28.sentence: Only {level}% of S&P 500 stocks are above their 200-day average, with the index {index_context}. Practitioners read narrow participation as a sign of fragility, though narrow, mega-cap-led markets have persisted for long stretches.
caveats: Practitioner indicator; weak academic evidence
Cap-weighted index concentration can keep breadth narrow for years

R29.condition: ema10 rises from < 0.40 to > 0.615 within 10 sessions
R29.sentence: A breadth thrust occurred: advancing issues surged from washed-out to strong participation within 10 days. StockCharts' review of 87 years of history shows mixed outcomes (10 'great', 3 'meh', 12 'horrible' signals), so it is a description, not a reliable buy signal.
caveats: Rare; mixed record; built on NYSE data only

R30.threshold_provenance: APP_HEURISTIC (use percentiles; levels drift with structural option growth)
R30.implies: Used as a contrarian gauge by practitioners. Academic evidence (Pan & Poteshman) is strong for stock-level, buyer-initiated opening volume, and weak or absent for aggregate index ratios.
R30.sentence: The equity put/call ratio's 10-day average is at an extreme ({pctile} percentile). Practitioners treat extremes as contrarian signals, but academic evidence for aggregate ratios is weak, so treat this as context rather than a signal.
caveats: 0DTE and ETF hedging have changed the ratio's composition
Index puts are often hedges, not directional bets

R31.implies: Baker-Wurgler-Yuan: sentiment is a contrarian predictor of market returns in aggregate. For the AAII survey specifically, US predictability largely disappeared after 1994 (Hengelbrock, Theissen, Westheide).
R31.sentence: The AAII bull-bear spread is {level}, an extreme reading. Sentiment research finds extremes have historically been weakly contrarian, but the AAII survey's predictive power has been inconsistent since the mid-1990s.
caveats: Small, self-selected weekly survey sample

R32.implies: Mixed evidence. Speculators tend to be trend followers (Boos & Grob), and speculative-pressure portfolios that FOLLOW net positioning earned positive excess returns (Fan et al. 2018). Extremes do raise squeeze/unwind risk when a catalyst hits (yen shorts before Aug 2024, per BIS).
R32.sentence: Speculative net positioning in {market} is at a {pctile} percentile extreme. Research does not support simply fading extremes, since speculators are often right on trend, but crowded positions have historically amplified moves when a shock forces an unwind.
caveats: Weekly data with a 3-day lag (Tuesday positions, Friday release)

R33.threshold_provenance: SOURCE (CNN bands, as reported by secondary sources)
R33.implies: Composite of 7 equal-weighted indicators (momentum, strength, breadth, put/call, junk bond demand, volatility, safe-haven demand). Redundant with the underlying inputs.
R33.sentence: The Fear & Greed index reads {level} ({band}). It is a composite of indicators already shown elsewhere in this brief and has no established academic track record as a timing tool.
caveats: Proprietary; double-counts VIX/put-call/breadth, so give it low weight in AI scoring

R34.implies: Defensive leadership with falling yields has historically accompanied growth scares. Cyclical leadership with rising yields accompanies reflation.
R34.sentence: Defensive sectors outperformed cyclicals by {spread}% over {window} while yields fell. Historically, this mix has accompanied growth worries, though sector moves also reflect earnings and positioning.
caveats: Sector composition changes (e.g. tech/communications reclassification)

R35.condition: kre_ret - spx_ret z <= -2 (regional bank stress) OR bank stocks rising with bear steepening
R35.implies: Fed research (English, Van den Heuvel, Zakrajšek): unexpected steepening raises NIMs, but rising long rates also cause capital losses on long-duration assets (visible in March 2023). The bank-stock reaction is ambiguous.
R35.sentence: Regional banks moved {chg}% as the curve {curve_move}. Fed research finds steeper curves have historically supported bank margins, but sharp rises in long rates can hurt banks through securities losses, so the net effect varies.
caveats: BoE and DNB find a weak slope-NIM link in other countries

R36.implies: The Russell 2000 carries far more floating-rate debt (about 30% per 2026 Bloomberg/Apollo data; older estimates higher) and higher interest/EBITDA than the S&P 500, and about 40% of constituents are unprofitable. Small caps have tended to outperform on falling front-end yields / dovish repricing and underperform on hawkish moves.
R36.sentence: Small caps {out_under}performed large caps by {spread}% as 2Y yields moved {chg2y}bp. Because small caps rely more on floating-rate debt, they have historically been more sensitive to Fed-path repricing than large caps.
caveats: Floating-rate share estimates vary widely by source/date
Small-cap rallies on cut hopes have often faded when cuts came with recession

R37.threshold_provenance: SOURCE (standardised surprise method, Andersen et al.); the 1 SD cutoff is APP_HEURISTIC
R37.implies: Surprises cause immediate price jumps. Bonds react most. Bad news moves prices more than good news (sign effect). Equity response depends on the cycle: in expansions, bad macro news has tended to be good for stocks via lower expected rates; in recessions, the opposite.
R37.sentence: {release} came in at {actual} vs {consensus} expected, a {std_surprise} standard-deviation surprise. Historically, bonds react most to such surprises. Whether stocks follow depends on whether markets read the news through a growth lens or a Fed lens.
caveats: Consensus quality varies
Revisions to prior months can dominate the headline

R38.condition: core CPI m/m surprise >= +0.1pp OR NFP surprise z >= 1, AND chg_2y on day >= +8bp (APP_HEURISTIC)
R38.implies: In inflation-dominated regimes, upside inflation/jobs surprises have lifted front-end yields and the dollar and pushed stocks down together (positive stock-bond correlation, 2022).
R38.sentence: {release} surprised by {surprise}, and 2Y yields moved {chg2y}bp. In inflation-focused regimes like 2022, hot data has historically pushed yields and the dollar up and stocks down together. In growth-focused regimes, strong data has been read more positively.
caveats: Regime-dependent (AQR/MSCI)

R39.threshold_provenance: SOURCE (ISM: >50 = manufacturing expanding; >42.3 sustained = overall economy generally expanding)
R39.implies: Below 50 = manufacturing contraction, but the overall economy has historically still grown above 42.3. A move back above 50 has historically been associated with cyclical/commodity outperformance and rising yields.
R39.sentence: ISM manufacturing is {level}. ISM notes readings above 50 indicate manufacturing expansion, and readings above 42.3 over time have generally been consistent with overall economic expansion.
caveats: Manufacturing is about 10% of GDP. ISM manufacturing was below 50 for long stretches in 2022-25 without recession

R40.condition: new_orders crosses 50 OR (new_orders - inventories) changes sign (APP_HEURISTIC)
R40.threshold_provenance: SOURCE for the 50 line (ISM diffusion index). The NO-minus-inventories spread is a practitioner CONVENTION
R40.sentence: ISM new orders are {level}. As a diffusion index, readings above 50 indicate more firms reporting rising orders, which practitioners treat as a leading component of the headline PMI.
caveats: Monthly noise; use 3-month average

R41.threshold_provenance: 400k = CONVENTION tested by the St. Louis Fed (they find the optimal threshold varies a lot over time; continuing-claims optimal average about 3m). 20% rise from trough = APP_HEURISTIC
R41.implies: Sustained rises in claims have historically signalled labour market weakening and rallied Treasuries. But many rises were not followed by recession (Richmond Fed found 26 such non-recession instances).
R41.sentence: The 4-week average of jobless claims is {level}k, up {chg_pct}% from its 12-month low. St. Louis Fed research finds claims can signal turning points, but no fixed threshold works across eras, and many past rises did not lead to recession.
caveats: Seasonal adjustment noise (holidays, auto retooling, hurricanes)
Claims are not an NBER dating criterion

R42.implies: Historically triggered early in every US recession since 1970, usually within a few months of onset. It is a real-time recession DATING indicator, not a predictor.
R42.sentence: The Sahm rule indicator is {level}pp (trigger at 0.50). Historically, crossing 0.50 has coincided with the early months of US recessions. It identifies recessions in real time rather than predicting them, and it triggered in August 2024 without a recession, partly because of labour-supply growth.
caveats: The 2024 trigger was a false positive / special case tied to immigration-driven labour supply
Unemployment rate revisions each January

R43.threshold_provenance: SOURCE (Conference Board: 80 historically signals recession within a year)
R43.sentence: The Conference Board Expectations Index is {level}, below the 80 level the Conference Board says has historically signalled recession ahead. The index has spent long stretches below 80 since 2022 without a recession, so it is a weak timing signal.
caveats: Sentiment-spending gap since 2022
Partisan and inflation-driven swings

R44.condition: lei_6m_diffusion < 50 AND lei_6m_ann_growth <= depth_threshold (about -4.0% to -4.4%, set per release)
R44.threshold_provenance: SOURCE (Conference Board 3Ds rule). Depth threshold varies by release
R44.sentence: The LEI's 6-month annualised change is {level}% with a diffusion of {diff}. When both criteria of the Conference Board's 3Ds rule are met, it has historically signalled recession, but the rule flashed through 2022-24 without one.
caveats: Goods/manufacturing-heavy components; long false signal in 2022-24

R45.condition: ebp_bp > 0 and rising (APP_HEURISTIC); EBP-implied recession prob from Fed model

R47.threshold_provenance: APP_HEURISTIC (price near par = strong demand is a CONVENTION; no official cutoff)
R47.implies: Loan prices near par and tight HY spreads have historically supported syndicated LBO financing, repricings and dividend recaps. Falling loan prices and HY spread spikes have historically pushed sponsors toward private credit or shelved deals.
R47.sentence: Leveraged loans average {price} and HY yields are {hy_yield}%. Historically, loan prices near par with tight spreads have marked open financing windows for leveraged M&A, while sharp spread widening has closed the syndicated market and shifted deals to private credit.
caveats: Private credit now finances a large share of LBOs (PitchBook LCD), so syndicated data understates availability
